How to Use This Book

A short map of the book, the three ways to read it, and the one rule that matters more than any technique.

4 min read·856 words·Start Here

Sex is one of the few important human activities we are expected to be good at without ever being taught. Most of us learn from pornography, jokes, rumor, and trial and error. That is a poor curriculum. It leaves people anxious about performance, unsure what their partner actually wants, and convinced that everyone else somehow received a manual they missed.

This book is that manual — not a script for a particular act, but a practical guide to the skills underneath good sex: consent, communication, attention, relaxation, and care. It is written for adults of any gender, orientation, or experience level. It assumes you want to be a better partner, not just a more impressive one.

Note · A note on scope

This book is educational. It is not medical advice, therapy, or a substitute for talking with a qualified professional about pain, sexual dysfunction, infection, or mental health. If something hurts, stops working, or worries you, get proper care. A good clinician will not be shocked.

What this book is #

A guide to the parts of sex that rarely make it into pornography: how to ask, how to listen, how to slow down, how to recover from awkward moments, and how to make pleasure mutual. It covers the practical basics — anatomy, arousal, foreplay, oral and manual stimulation, penetration, stamina, pelvic-floor health, aftercare — but the thread running through every chapter is the same: good sex is collaborative, consensual, and responsive.

It is also deliberately non-graphic. You will find clear explanations and practical principles, not a shot-by-shot script or explicit scenes. The aim is understanding, not titillation.

What this book is not #

It is not a collection of tricks for manipulating someone into bed. It is not a promise that one technique works on every body. It is not a ranking of bodies, acts, or orientations. And it is not a substitute for the most important source of information you have: the person in front of you.

Research on sex is often based on heterosexual, cisgender couples, college students, or people comfortable answering questionnaires. Where the evidence is thin, this book says so. Where patterns are common but not universal, it uses words like many, most, and some rather than all or always. Your partner is not a statistic. Neither are you.

Three ways to read it #

Straight through. Read the foundations first, then the practice chapters. The book is designed to build in that order, and the later chapters refer back to ideas introduced early.

By problem. If you are dealing with a specific issue — rushing, anxiety, difficulty lasting, trouble communicating — jump to that chapter. Each one stands on its own, and the contents page is detailed enough to find the right door.

As a reference. Keep it nearby. Use the scripts and checklists in Appendix A, the myths in Appendix B, and the pelvic-floor routine in Appendix C when you need them. You do not have to remember everything. You just have to be willing to look things up.

The one rule #

If you remember nothing else, remember this:

Consent is not a box you tick at the start. It is a conversation that continues for as long as the sex does.

Consent is freely given, reversible, informed, enthusiastic, and specific. It can be withdrawn at any moment, for any reason, or for no reason at all. A yes to one thing is not a yes to another. A yes last week is not a yes tonight. Silence is not consent. Pressure is not consent. Being in a relationship is not consent.

The rest of this book assumes that rule. Every technique, every script, every suggestion is built on it.

A note on language #

Sexual anatomy is not destiny, and not everyone has the same body or uses the same words for it. This book uses people with vulvas and people with penises when the anatomy matters, and partners when it does not. It also uses women and men when summarizing research that used those categories, because that is how the research was conducted — not because those categories describe everyone.

You will not find assumptions about who should initiate, who should penetrate, who should orgasm first, or what a "normal" sex life looks like. There is no normal. There is only what is safe, wanted, and satisfying for the people involved.

How to use the checklists #

Several chapters end with a short checklist. They are prompts, not exams. Tick what is useful, ignore what is not, and treat the unchecked boxes as questions to discuss rather than failures. The HTML edition remembers your ticks in the browser; the print and EPUB editions are for paper or e-reader notes.

Tip · Start small

You do not have to change everything at once. Pick one chapter, one conversation, or one habit. Consistency beats intensity — in sex, as in most things.

A final word before Chapter 1 #

You are not broken, behind, or fundamentally bad at this. Most people are under-taught, over-exposed to unrealistic images, and rarely given a chance to practice the unglamorous skills that make sex good: asking, listening, pacing, laughing, and trying again.

That is fixable. Let's begin.

Better Sex Is a Skill, Not a Performance

Why the performance mindset makes sex worse, and what to replace it with.

5 min read·1,185 words·Part I — Foundations

Most people carry a hidden scoreboard into bed. Did I last long enough? Did they come? Was I impressive? Did I do the right thing? The questions are understandable — we are social animals, and sex feels like a test of competence — but they are also the fastest way to ruin a good time.

The scoreboard turns sex into a performance. A performance has an audience, a script, and a verdict. It rewards appearance over connection, technique over attention, and outcome over experience. It makes you self-conscious at exactly the moment you need to be present. And it turns your partner into a judge rather than a collaborator.

This chapter is about replacing that mindset with something more useful: sex as a skill.

Skill is not the same as technique #

A technique is a move. A skill is a capacity. Techniques are useful, but they are context-dependent: what works for one person on one night may not work for another. Skills are portable. They include:

  • Attention — noticing what is happening in your partner's body, breath, and voice.
  • Communication — asking, telling, and adjusting in real time.
  • Pacing — knowing when to speed up, slow down, pause, or change course.
  • Self-regulation — managing anxiety, excitement, and the urge to rush.
  • Recovery — handling awkward moments without spiraling.
  • Care — treating your partner's comfort and pleasure as part of your own.

These are learnable. They improve with practice and feedback. They do not depend on having the right body, the right experience, or the right script.

The performance trap #

The performance mindset shows up in predictable ways.

Spectatoring. You watch yourself from the outside, monitoring your performance instead of feeling the moment. Am I doing this right? Do I look stupid? Are they bored? The more you watch, the less you feel, and the less you feel, the harder it becomes to respond.

Outcome obsession. You fixate on a specific ending — an orgasm, a particular position, a number of minutes — and treat anything else as failure. This is especially common around orgasm, stamina, and erection. It turns sex into a pass/fail exam and makes the "failure" more likely.

Comparison. You measure yourself against pornography, an ex, a fantasy, or a story someone told. Porn is edited, staged, and designed to look effortless. It is not a documentary. Neither is your memory of someone else's highlight reel.

Mind reading. You assume you know what your partner wants, or you expect them to know what you want without being told. Both assumptions are unfair. Bodies and preferences are not standardized.

Scorekeeping. You count orgasms, positions, or minutes and use the numbers to judge the encounter. Sex is not a sport, and your partner is not a leaderboard.

Watch out · The paradox

The harder you try to perform, the less present you become — and the less present you are, the worse the sex feels for both of you. Relaxation is not the opposite of effort. It is the condition that makes good effort possible.

What skill looks like in practice #

A skilled lover is not someone who knows every move. A skilled lover is someone who can answer three questions in real time:

  1. What is happening right now? (Attention)
  2. What does my partner want more or less of? (Communication)
  3. What should I do next? (Adjustment)

That is the whole loop. It sounds simple because it is simple. It is hard because it requires you to stop performing and start paying attention.

The skill loop #

Notice. Pay attention to breath, muscle tension, sounds, movement, and the words your partner uses — or does not use. Notice your own body too. Are you rushing? Clenching? Holding your breath?

Ask. When you are unsure, ask. When you are fairly sure, check in anyway. "Do you like this?" "Harder or softer?" "Do you want more of this, or something else?" The questions do not have to be clinical. They can be whispered, playful, or direct.

Adjust. Change one thing at a time. Speed, pressure, angle, rhythm, location, or position. Then notice again. Small adjustments are easier to read than dramatic changes.

Check in again. Sex is not a linear checklist. It is a loop. What worked two minutes ago may not work now. Keep returning to the loop.

The goal is not orgasm #

Orgasm is great. It is also not the only point of sex, and it is not a reliable measure of whether sex was good. Many people have satisfying sex without orgasm. Many people have orgasms during sex that still feels disconnected or unsatisfying. And many people feel pressure to orgasm precisely because a partner is treating it as the finish line.

A better goal is mutual pleasure and connection — the sense that both people were seen, wanted, and cared for. Orgasm may be part of that. It may not be. Either way, the encounter can be good.

This matters for men in particular, because the performance mindset often trains men to treat their own orgasm as the end of sex and their partner's orgasm as a box to tick. Both assumptions reduce pleasure. Sex does not end when one person comes. It ends when the people involved decide it ends.

Enthusiasm beats expertise #

If you watch people talk about their best sexual experiences, the same words come up again and again: wanted, safe, present, generous, funny, responsive. Not technically impressive. Not perfect.

Enthusiasm is a skill. It looks like:

  • Saying what you like instead of hoping your partner guesses.
  • Showing that you are into them with words, sounds, and touch.
  • Laughing when something is awkward instead of pretending it did not happen.
  • Asking for what you want without apologizing for having desires.
  • Being genuinely curious about your partner's body and preferences.

You do not have to be confident every second. You just have to be willing to participate.

A practice mindset #

Skills improve through practice, and practice requires permission to be imperfect. That means:

  • Start where you are. You do not need to be experienced to be attentive.
  • Choose one thing. Pick one skill from this chapter — asking, pacing, or noticing — and practice it for a week.
  • Get feedback. Ask your partner what felt good. Ask what they wanted more of. Listen without defending.
  • Expect awkwardness. New things are awkward. Awkwardness is not a sign that you are doing it wrong; it is a sign that you are doing something new.
  • Recover quickly. If something does not work, say so, laugh if you can, and try something else. The ability to recover is more valuable than the ability to avoid mistakes.

Key idea · The shift

Stop asking, Did I perform well? Start asking, Were we both here? The first question makes you anxious. The second makes you attentive.

What to take into the next chapter #

Sex is a skill, not a performance. The goal is not to execute a perfect routine; it is to create an experience that is safe, mutual, and alive. That requires attention, communication, and the willingness to adjust.

The next chapter goes deeper into the foundation that makes all of that possible: consent, communication, and safety. Without them, technique is just noise.

Consent, Communication, and Safety

The conversations that make everything else easier — and the safety rules that are not optional.

7 min read·1,672 words·Part I — Foundations

If sex is a skill, communication is the skill. Not the smooth, scripted kind of communication you see in movies, where people always know what to say and never feel awkward. The real kind: asking, answering, admitting uncertainty, changing your mind, and trying again.

This chapter covers three things that belong together: consent, communication, and safety. They are not separate boxes. Consent depends on communication. Safety depends on both. And all three depend on treating your partner as a person rather than a puzzle to solve.

Consent is a practice #

Consent is often described as a single question at the start of sex: Is this okay? That is a good start, but it is not enough. Consent is ongoing. It can change. It can be withdrawn. It can be specific to one act, one moment, or one mood.

The most useful model is FRIES:

LetterMeaningWhat it sounds like
FFreely givenNo pressure, manipulation, guilt, or fear.
RReversibleAnyone can change their mind, at any time.
IInformedEveryone knows what they are agreeing to.
EEnthusiasticA genuine yes, not a reluctant maybe.
SSpecificA yes to one thing is not a yes to everything.

Watch out · Silence is not consent

A person who is frozen, quiet, uncomfortable, or going along with something is not automatically consenting. If you are unsure, stop and ask. The momentary awkwardness of checking is always better than the lasting harm of assuming.

What consent sounds like #

Consent does not have to be formal. It can be playful, direct, or nonverbal — as long as it is clear. Some examples:

  • "I want to kiss you. Is that okay?"
  • "Do you want me to keep going?"
  • "I'm into this, but I don't want to do X tonight. Is that alright?"
  • "Can I touch you here?"
  • "That feels good. Do you want more?"
  • "I need to stop. Can we pause?"

Nonverbal cues matter too: nodding, pulling closer, guiding a hand, making sounds of pleasure. But nonverbal cues can be ambiguous, especially with a new partner or during a charged moment. When in doubt, use words.

When consent is not consent #

Consent is not valid when someone is:

  • Asleep, unconscious, or unable to communicate clearly.
  • Severely intoxicated or under the influence of drugs.
  • Being pressured, threatened, guilt-tripped, or manipulated.
  • Afraid of the consequences of saying no.
  • Underage.
  • Agreeing to something they do not understand or have not been informed about.

A prior yes does not override a current no. A relationship does not create blanket access. Flirting, kissing, or removing clothes is not consent to anything further. Consent is a continuing conversation, not a contract.

Checking in without killing the mood #

One of the most common fears is that asking will ruin the moment. In practice, the opposite is usually true: a well-timed check-in signals care, confidence, and attentiveness. It can even be sexy.

Try:

  • "Do you like that?"
  • "Harder or softer?"
  • "Right there?"
  • "Do you want more, or should I slow down?"
  • "What would feel good right now?"
  • "I want to try something. Want to hear it?"

Keep your tone warm, curious, and unhurried. You are not conducting an interview. You are staying connected.

Communication is a loop #

Good sexual communication is not a single speech. It is a loop: ask, tell, adjust, check in. The same loop from Chapter 1 applies here.

Ask. Find out what your partner wants, likes, or is curious about. Ask open questions when possible: "What do you enjoy?" "What would you like more of?" "Is there anything you want to try?"

Tell. Say what you want too. Your pleasure matters. "I like that." "A little slower." "I want you to touch me here." Telling is not demanding. It is giving your partner useful information.

Adjust. Change something based on what you heard. Speed, pressure, position, rhythm, or focus. Then notice what happens.

Check in. Keep the loop going. Sex is dynamic. What worked five minutes ago may not work now.

Giving feedback #

Feedback is easier to hear when it is specific, timely, and framed positively.

  • Specific: "A little more pressure on the left" is easier to act on than "do it better."
  • Timely: Say it in the moment when possible. "That's good — keep doing that" is more useful than a post-game critique.
  • Positive: Start with what is working. "I love that. Can you do it a little slower?" is easier to receive than "you're going too fast."

You can also use the compliment sandwich outside the bedroom: something you appreciated, something you would like to try differently, and something you are looking forward to. It sounds corny, but it works.

Receiving feedback #

Feedback is a gift, even when it is awkward. Try to:

  • Listen without defending. Let your partner finish.
  • Thank them. "Thanks for telling me" is a complete sentence.
  • Ask for clarification. "Can you show me what you mean?"
  • Adjust without sulking. You are not being criticized as a person; you are being given information about a preference.
  • Follow up. "Was that better?" shows that you were paying attention.

If you feel hurt or embarrassed, say so later, outside the bedroom. Do not punish your partner for being honest.

Tip · The 24-hour rule

If a conversation is too charged in the moment, pause it and agree to come back within 24 hours. "I want to talk about this, but I need a little time. Can we talk tomorrow?" is better than forcing a conversation that turns into a fight.

Safety is part of pleasure #

Safety is not the opposite of spontaneity. It is what makes spontaneity possible. When people feel safe — physically, emotionally, and sexually — they relax. Relaxation is a prerequisite for arousal and pleasure.

Physical safety #

  • STI protection. Condoms and dental dams reduce the risk of many sexually transmitted infections. They are not a comment on anyone's cleanliness. They are basic care.
  • Contraception. If pregnancy is a possibility, use a method that works for you and discuss it before sex, not after.
  • Lubrication. Friction is not a virtue. Use lubricant. Water-based lubricant is compatible with most condoms and toys; silicone-based lubricant lasts longer but can damage silicone toys.
  • Clean hands and toys. Wash hands, trim nails, and clean toys before and after use. Use condoms on toys when sharing.
  • Pain is information, not a challenge. If something hurts, stop. Adjust. If pain persists, see a healthcare provider.
  • Allergies and sensitivities. Check lubricants, condoms, and toys for ingredients that may irritate.

Emotional safety #

  • No pressure. Enthusiastic consent cannot coexist with pressure, guilt, or threats.
  • No surprises. Do not introduce a new act, toy, or boundary without checking first.
  • No humiliation unless it is explicitly negotiated. Rough play, restraint, and power exchange require clear consent, safe words, and aftercare.
  • No revenge. Do not use sex, withdrawal, or affection as punishment.
  • No secrets that affect consent. If you have an STI, disclose it before sex. If you are not free to consent — because you are in a monogamous relationship with someone else, for example — say so.

Alcohol and drugs #

A drink or two can lower inhibitions. Too much can make consent impossible. If someone is slurring, unsteady, confused, or unable to communicate clearly, they cannot consent. Do not have sex with them. Help them get home safely instead.

If you are the one who has been drinking, remember that your own judgment is impaired. Decide your boundaries before you drink, and respect them in the morning.

Safe words and check-ins #

If you explore power exchange, restraint, or intense sensation, agree on a safe word before you start. A safe word is a word that means stop immediately, no negotiation. "No" and "stop" should always mean stop; a safe word is an additional, unmistakable signal.

The traffic-light system is simple and widely used:

  • Green: Keep going. I'm enjoying this.
  • Yellow: Slow down or check in. I'm approaching a limit.
  • Red: Stop now.

Agree on what happens after a red light: stop the scene, comfort, water, blanket, talk. Aftercare is not optional.

Note · Not everyone needs a safe word

Safe words are essential for power exchange and intense play. For ordinary sex, "stop" and "no" should be enough. If your partner does not feel able to say stop, that is a sign to slow down and check in.

The conversation before the conversation #

The best time to talk about sex is often when you are not having it. A calm, private conversation — over coffee, on a walk, in bed after the lights are out — can cover:

  • What you each enjoy and want more of.
  • What you are curious about trying.
  • What is off the table.
  • How you will signal discomfort or a need to stop.
  • STI status, testing, and contraception.
  • What aftercare looks like for each of you.

This conversation does not have to be a formal summit. It can be playful. "I was thinking about what I want to try with you" is a great opener. So is "Is there anything you've been wanting but haven't asked for?"

Repair matters more than perfect communication #

You will misread signals. You will say the wrong thing. You will have a moment that lands badly. That is normal. What matters is repair.

Repair sounds like:

  • "I'm sorry. I moved too fast. Are you okay?"
  • "I didn't mean to pressure you. Let's stop."
  • "I heard you say no, and I kept going. That was wrong. What do you need now?"
  • "I'm feeling embarrassed, but I want to understand what you meant."

Repair is not about being perfect. It is about being accountable. Couples who repair well tend to have better sex than couples who never make mistakes — because they can recover from the inevitable ones.

Key idea · The foundation

Consent, communication, and safety are not the boring prerequisites to the "real" sex. They are the conditions that make pleasure possible. Get them right, and everything else gets easier.

Anatomy and Arousal: A Practical Map

A plain-language map of the body, the arousal cycle, and why individual variation matters more than any diagram.

6 min read·1,431 words·Part I — Foundations

Most people learn anatomy from slang, pornography, and a few awkward diagrams. The result is a lot of confidence about the wrong things and a lot of uncertainty about the right ones. This chapter is a reset: a clear, non-graphic map of the parts involved in sex, what they do, and why no two people respond in exactly the same way.

You do not need to memorize every term. You do need to understand that bodies are not standardized, that arousal is not a simple on/off switch, and that the most reliable guide to a partner's body is their own feedback.

The vulva is not the vagina #

A common mistake is using vagina to describe everything external. The vagina is the internal canal. The vulva is the entire external genital area. It includes:

  • The mons pubis — the fleshy pad over the pubic bone.
  • The labia majora — the outer lips.
  • The labia minora — the inner lips, which vary enormously in size, shape, and color.
  • The clitoris — the primary organ of sexual pleasure for most people with vulvas. The visible glans is only the tip; the internal structure extends into the body.
  • The vestibule — the area around the vaginal and urethral openings.
  • The urethra — the tube that carries urine, separate from the vagina.
  • The vaginal opening — where the vagina meets the vulva.
  • The perineum — the area between the vulva and the anus.
  • The anus — an opening with its own nerve supply and, for some people, its own pleasure potential.

The clitoris deserves special attention. It is not a small button on the surface; it is a larger structure with internal shafts and bulbs that wrap around the vaginal opening. It contains a very high concentration of nerve endings. For most people with vulvas, clitoral stimulation is the most reliable route to orgasm.

The vagina is a muscular canal. It has fewer concentrated nerve endings than the clitoris, and its sensitivity varies. Many people experience pleasure from penetration because it stimulates the internal clitoris, the surrounding tissues, or the pelvic floor — not because the vaginal walls are uniformly sensitive.

The cervix is the opening of the uterus at the top of the vagina. It can be sensitive, and deep penetration may feel uncomfortable for some people. That is information, not a failure.

The penis and surrounding structures #

The external penis consists of:

  • The glans — the head, which is highly sensitive.
  • The shaft — the body of the penis.
  • The foreskin — a fold of skin that covers the glans in uncircumcised people. It can be retracted or left in place, depending on comfort and preference.
  • The scrotum and testicles — sensitive, but not always in the way pornography suggests.
  • The perineum — the area between the scrotum and the anus, which can be sensitive.
  • The prostate — a gland below the bladder that can be stimulated through the anal wall. This requires explicit consent, hygiene, lubrication, and a willing partner. It is not for everyone, and that is fine.

The pelvic floor is a hammock of muscles that supports the bladder, bowel, and reproductive organs. It plays a role in erection, ejaculation, orgasm, and continence for people of all genders. Chapter 8 covers pelvic-floor training in detail.

The CUV complex #

You may have heard of the "G-spot" — a supposedly distinct spot on the front vaginal wall that produces intense pleasure. The evidence is more complicated. Anatomical studies have not consistently found a discrete structure that matches the popular description. What many people are feeling is probably the clitourethrovaginal (CUV) complex: the internal clitoris, the urethra and surrounding tissue, and the front wall of the vagina, all connected by nerves, blood vessels, and connective tissue.

This matters for two reasons. First, it shifts the focus from hunting for a mythical button to exploring a responsive region. Second, it explains why the same stimulation can feel different from person to person, and even from one day to another.

The Skene's glands — sometimes called the paraurethral glands — sit near the urethra and are homologous to the male prostate. They produce a small amount of fluid in some people during arousal or orgasm. This is distinct from the larger-volume fluid release often called "squirting," which research suggests comes primarily from the bladder. Both are normal variations. Neither is a measure of skill, intensity, or intimacy. Do not make fluid release a goal; if it happens, fine. If it does not, fine.

Note · No universal map

There is no spot, angle, or technique that works for everyone. The CUV complex is a useful concept, not a cheat code. Explore gently, ask for feedback, and let your partner's responses guide you.

The arousal cycle #

A common model describes sexual response in stages: desire, excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution. It is useful as a rough map, but it is not a script. Many people skip stages, cycle back, plateau for a long time, or never reach orgasm. Some people experience desire only after arousal begins — a pattern sometimes called responsive desire.

A more realistic model is a loop:

Desire can come before, during, or after arousal. It can be spontaneous ("I want sex now") or responsive ("I feel interested once we start"). Neither is more valid.

Excitement involves increased blood flow, lubrication, swelling, sensitivity, faster breathing, and muscle tension. It builds with stimulation, but it also depends on safety, attention, and mood.

Plateau is the sustained high-arousal phase. It can last seconds or a long time. Many people need consistent stimulation to stay there.

Orgasm is a rhythmic release of muscle tension, often accompanied by intense pleasure and involuntary contractions. It is not required for good sex, and it is not always easy to reach.

Resolution is the aftermath: relaxation, sensitivity, and a return to baseline. Some people can continue and have multiple orgasms; others need a break. Both are normal.

Arousal non-concordance #

One of the most important ideas in this book: genital response and subjective arousal do not always match.

A person can be physically lubricated or erect without feeling turned on. A person can feel intensely aroused without obvious physical signs. This is called arousal non-concordance. It is normal, and it is especially important for understanding consent.

It means:

  • An erection is not consent.
  • Lubrication is not consent.
  • A lack of physical response is not a verdict on your attractiveness.
  • "My body is responding" does not necessarily mean "I want this."

Consent is about what a person wants and agrees to, not what their body is doing automatically. If you are unsure, ask.

What most people need #

Research on orgasm consistently finds that clitoral stimulation is the most reliable route for most people with vulvas. Estimates vary, but only a minority — often cited as around 18% — report that penetration alone is reliably sufficient for orgasm. Many more need direct or indirect clitoral stimulation, alone or combined with penetration.

That does not mean penetration is unimportant. It means penetration is one part of a larger picture. Pleasure can come from:

  • Clitoral stimulation (fingers, mouth, toys, grinding, or pressure through the vulva).
  • Internal stimulation (fingers, penetration, or toys).
  • Combined stimulation (clitoral plus internal, which many people find most reliable).
  • Whole-body touch, kissing, massage, and anticipation.
  • Psychological factors: feeling desired, safe, seen, and free from pressure.

Preferences for pressure, rhythm, location, and speed vary enormously. Some people like light, indirect touch; others want firm, consistent pressure. Some want a steady rhythm; others want variation. The only way to know is to ask and observe.

Watch out · Porn is not a guide

Pornography is entertainment. It is edited, staged, and designed to look visually dramatic, not to represent what most people enjoy. It often skips foreplay, ignores clitoral stimulation, and treats orgasm as a performance. Use it as fantasy if you like, not as an instruction manual.

Orgasm is not the whole story #

Orgasm can be intense, pleasurable, and connecting. It can also be elusive, especially under pressure. Many people have satisfying sex without orgasm. Many people have orgasms that feel mechanical or disconnected. Pleasure is broader than the peak.

A useful question is not "Did we orgasm?" but "Did we feel good? Did we feel close? Did we want to do that again?" Those questions leave room for all kinds of bodies and all kinds of endings.

The takeaway #

Bodies vary. Arousal varies. Pleasure varies. The map in this chapter is a starting point, not a rulebook. The most important anatomical fact is that your partner's body is specific, and the most important skill is learning it through attention and communication.

Presence, Pressure, and Confidence

How to get out of your head, manage performance pressure, and be confident without pretending to know everything.

6 min read·1,271 words·Part I — Foundations

The biggest sex organ is the brain. That is a cliché because it is true. Desire, arousal, pleasure, and orgasm all depend on the nervous system — and the nervous system is not very cooperative when it feels judged.

This chapter is about the mental game: the anxiety, self-criticism, and pressure that pull you out of the moment, and the practical ways to come back.

The spectator #

The most common mental obstacle is spectatoring — watching yourself from the outside during sex. You become both participant and critic:

Am I doing this right? Should I change position? Am I taking too long? Do they think I'm boring? Is my body weird? Why isn't this working?

The spectator is trying to help. It wants you to perform well. But it is a terrible lover. It pulls attention away from sensation, from your partner, and from the actual moment. The more you watch, the less you feel. The less you feel, the more you worry. The more you worry, the worse it gets.

How to step off the balcony #

You cannot force the spectator to leave. You can give it something else to do.

  • Name it. "I'm in my head." Naming the pattern reduces its power.
  • Return to sensation. Notice one physical sensation: the temperature of your partner's skin, the pressure of their hand, the rhythm of your breath.
  • Slow down. Anxiety lives in speed. Slow your breathing, your movements, and your expectations.
  • Look at your partner. Make eye contact. Notice their face. Reconnect with the person rather than the performance.
  • Say something. "I'm a little in my head. Can we slow down?" Honesty is disarming — for both of you.

Tip · The 5-4-3-2-1 ground

If anxiety is spiraling, silently name five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell, and one you can taste. It sounds like a party trick, but it pulls attention back into the body and the room.

Performance pressure #

Performance pressure comes from a reasonable place: you want to be good. But it quickly becomes counterproductive. It turns sex into an evaluation and makes every moment carry the weight of a verdict.

Common forms of pressure:

  • The orgasm mandate. "I have to make them come."
  • The stamina mandate. "I have to last a certain amount of time."
  • The erection mandate. "I have to stay hard the whole time."
  • The technique mandate. "I have to know exactly what I'm doing."
  • The body mandate. "I have to look good from every angle."

Each of these is a standard you have invented or absorbed. None of them is a requirement for good sex. And all of them make you less present.

Replace the mandate with a question #

Instead of Did I perform? ask What is happening right now, and what would feel good next? The first question is about your ego. The second is about the shared experience.

You can also give yourself permission out loud:

  • "I don't have to be perfect. I just have to be here."
  • "We can stop whenever we want."
  • "Orgasm is not the finish line."
  • "If something doesn't work, we can laugh and try something else."

Confidence is not certainty #

People often think confidence means knowing exactly what to do. It does not. Confidence means being comfortable enough with uncertainty to act anyway.

A confident lover can say:

  • "I don't know what you like yet. Show me."
  • "I've never tried that. Want to explore it together?"
  • "That didn't work. Let's try something else."
  • "I'm nervous, but I'm glad we're here."

That is not weakness. It is honesty, and honesty is attractive because it makes room for the other person to be honest too.

The confidence loop #

Confidence grows through action, not affirmation. You build it by:

  1. Doing the thing — initiating a conversation, asking for what you want, trying something new.
  2. Surviving the awkwardness — noticing that nothing catastrophic happened.
  3. Learning — adjusting based on feedback.
  4. Repeating — building evidence that you can handle uncertainty.

You do not need to feel confident before you act. You become confident by acting, imperfectly, and living to tell the tale.

Body image #

Many people worry about their bodies during sex: stomach, thighs, chest, scars, hair, smell, sounds, wrinkles, disability, or size. The worry pulls attention away from pleasure and into self-monitoring.

Some practical responses:

  • Remember that your partner is not grading you. They are usually far more focused on their own experience — and on you as a person — than on the flaws you are cataloging.
  • Ask for reassurance if you need it. "I'm feeling self-conscious. Can you tell me what you like about my body?" is a vulnerable, legitimate request.
  • Dim the lights if it helps, but do not hide. Hiding reinforces the idea that your body is unacceptable. You are allowed to take up space.
  • Talk back to the critic. Would you say those things to someone you love? Then do not say them to yourself.
  • Seek support if body image is severely affecting your life. Therapy can help, and there is no shame in it.

Erection and arousal worries #

For people with penises, anxiety about erections can become a self-fulfilling prophecy. Worry activates the sympathetic nervous system — the fight-or-flight branch — which is the opposite of what erection requires. The more you monitor, the less reliable it becomes.

Helpful reframes:

  • An erection is not a measure of desire. Arousal non-concordance works both ways. You can be attracted and not erect; you can be erect and not interested.
  • Take a break. Stop trying to force it. Focus on your partner, on touch, on pleasure without penetration. Often the erection returns when the pressure drops.
  • Use what you have. Hands, mouth, toys, and closeness are not consolation prizes. They are sex.
  • Talk about it. "I'm in my head about this. Can we slow down?" is better than silently spiraling.
  • See a doctor if it persists. Erectile difficulties can have physical causes — cardiovascular health, medication, hormones, sleep, stress. A clinician can help.

Premature ejaculation worries #

If you ejaculate sooner than you want, you are not alone. It is one of the most common sexual concerns. It is also treatable. Chapter 8 covers practical techniques; the mental piece belongs here.

  • Do not apologize repeatedly. One "sorry, that was fast" is enough. Excessive apology makes your partner manage your feelings.
  • Reframe it as information. "I was more excited than I expected. Give me a few minutes and let's keep going" is confident and honest.
  • Remember that sex is not over. You have hands, a mouth, toys, and time. Your orgasm is not the closing bell.
  • Do not compare yourself to porn. Porn depicts edited, staged endurance. It is not a baseline.

Humor and humility #

Sex is absurd. Bodies make noises. Positions fail. Someone gets a cramp. A cat walks across the bed. The ability to laugh — kindly, not cruelly — is a superpower.

Humor works when it is:

  • Shared, not aimed at your partner.
  • Gentle, not mocking.
  • Brief, not a deflection from a real issue.
  • Followed by reconnection, not a retreat into jokes.

Humility works too. You are not supposed to know everything. You are supposed to be curious. "I have no idea what I'm doing, but I'm enjoying figuring it out with you" is a surprisingly good line.

Key idea · The mental shift

You do not need to be flawless. You need to be present, curious, and kind — to your partner and to yourself. Confidence is what happens when you stop auditioning and start participating.

Foreplay and the Art of Build-Up

Why the part before sex is not a warm-up, and how to make it worth staying for.

5 min read·1,175 words·Part II — The Practice

Foreplay has a branding problem. The word itself suggests it is preliminary — something you do before the main event. That framing is both inaccurate and unhelpful. For many people, foreplay is the main event. For almost everyone, it is what makes the main event possible.

This chapter is about build-up: the touch, attention, anticipation, and pacing that turn sex from a transaction into an experience.

Foreplay is sex #

The distinction between foreplay and sex is arbitrary. Kissing, touching, teasing, oral, and manual stimulation are not appetizers before the "real" act. They are sex. They can be the whole encounter, or they can lead somewhere else. Either is valid.

This matters because the foreplay-as-warm-up mindset creates a checklist: a few minutes of kissing, a bit of touching, then on to penetration. That approach rushes the part that many people need most. It also reinforces the idea that penetration is the only thing that counts.

A better framing: build-up is the process of increasing arousal, connection, and anticipation. It can include:

  • Conversation, flirting, and anticipation before you even touch.
  • Kissing and prolonged making out.
  • Whole-body touch, massage, and teasing.
  • Oral and manual stimulation.
  • Toys, role-play, or power exchange, if consensual and negotiated.
  • Music, lighting, privacy, and comfort.

Note · Time is not a scoreboard

There is no correct number of minutes. Some people need a long, slow build-up; others are ready quickly. The right amount is the amount that feels good to both of you — not a number you read in a magazine.

The 10-minute rule #

A useful starting point: spend at least ten minutes on non-genital touch before heading between the legs. Not because ten is magic, but because it interrupts the rush.

Non-genital touch can include:

  • Kissing the mouth, neck, ears, collarbones, shoulders, and back.
  • Stroking the arms, hands, thighs, and stomach.
  • Massage with warm oil or lotion.
  • Hair stroking, scalp massage, or gentle scratching.
  • Teasing touch that moves close to erogenous zones and then away again.
  • Eye contact, whispered words, and breathing together.

The goal is not to delay penetration as a test of willpower. The goal is to let arousal build gradually, so the body has time to respond and the mind has time to arrive.

Kissing #

Kissing is underrated. It is one of the most intimate things people do, and it is a reliable way to gauge chemistry and consent. A good kiss is not a performance; it is a conversation.

Principles:

  • Start slow. A gentle kiss is easier to respond to than an immediate invasion.
  • Match and vary. Follow your partner's rhythm, then introduce small variations.
  • Use your hands. Cupping a face, holding a waist, or stroking a neck adds connection.
  • Pay attention. If they pull back, slow down. If they lean in, continue.
  • Do not forget lips, necks, and ears. The mouth is not the only destination.

Touch and teasing #

Teasing is the art of building anticipation. It works by creating a gap between wanting and getting — a gap that is pleasurable as long as it is consensual and not frustrating.

Examples:

  • Stroking the inner thigh and moving away before reaching the genitals.
  • Kissing around the mouth without quite kissing it.
  • Light touch that becomes firmer as arousal builds.
  • Describing what you want to do, then doing it slowly.
  • Pausing to look at your partner, smile, or ask a question.

Teasing requires calibration. Some people love it; others find it annoying or anxiety-provoking. Watch for signs of frustration, and check in. "Do you want me to keep teasing, or do you want more?" is a useful question.

Massage #

A full-body massage is one of the most reliable forms of foreplay because it combines relaxation, touch, and attention without demanding performance. It also gives you a way to explore your partner's body respectfully.

A simple sequence:

  1. Set up. Warm room, comfortable surface, oil or lotion, towels, privacy.
  2. Ask. "Do you want a massage? Any areas to avoid?"
  3. Start broad. Back, shoulders, arms, legs — firm, slow strokes.
  4. Vary pressure. Ask what feels good. Use palms, thumbs, and fingertips.
  5. Build toward sensitive areas. Inner thighs, lower back, stomach, chest — but only with consent and attention.
  6. Do not treat it as a transaction. The massage is not a down payment on sex. It is pleasure in its own right.

Oral and manual stimulation #

Oral and manual sex are covered in detail in the next chapter. In the context of build-up, the key principles are:

  • Do not rush. Start slow and build.
  • Ask for feedback. "More pressure? Slower?"
  • Combine. Hands and mouth together are often more effective than either alone.
  • Do not treat it as a countdown. If your partner is enjoying it, stay. If they want something else, move.

The environment #

Environment is not everything, but it is not nothing. A comfortable, private, warm space helps people relax. Consider:

  • Privacy. Nothing kills arousal like the fear of being walked in on.
  • Temperature. Cold rooms make bodies tense.
  • Lighting. Some people feel more confident in dim light; others want to see.
  • Cleanliness. Fresh sheets, a shower, and clean hands are basic care.
  • Sound. Music can mask awkward silences and set a mood, but not everyone wants a soundtrack.
  • Comfort. A pillow under the hips, a blanket, or a glass of water can make a surprising difference.

None of these are requirements. They are small ways to signal that you care about the experience.

Common foreplay mistakes #

Rushing to the genitals. The clitoris and penis are not the only sensitive areas. The whole body is.

Treating foreplay as a checklist. Kiss, touch, oral, penetration — in that order. Bodies do not follow scripts.

Ignoring feedback. If your partner says "slower" or "harder," adjust. Do not keep doing what you were doing because it worked last time.

Making it one-sided. Foreplay is not something you do to your partner before they do something to you. It is mutual. Ask for what you want too.

Forgetting the mind. Arousal starts before touch. Flirting, anticipation, and feeling desired matter.

Not asking. Assuming you know what your partner likes is the most common mistake of all.

Tip · The pause

When you notice yourself rushing, pause. Stop moving. Breathe. Look at your partner. Ask, "What do you want right now?" The pause is not a setback. It is a reset.

Build-up for different bodies #

The principles apply broadly, but the specifics vary.

People with vulvas often need more time, more clitoral stimulation, and more whole-body touch. Many need direct clitoral stimulation to orgasm, with or without penetration.

People with penises often respond to firm, rhythmic stimulation, but anxiety and pressure can interfere. Slowing down and reducing performance demands can help.

Everyone benefits from feeling desired, safe, and attended to. That is not a technique. It is a condition.

The takeaway #

Foreplay is not the price of admission to sex. It is sex. The goal is not to endure it until the "real" part; it is to make the whole encounter worth being present for. Slow down, pay attention, and let the build-up be part of the pleasure.

Oral, Hands, and Giving Pleasure

Practical principles for giving pleasure with your mouth and hands — without turning it into a routine.

6 min read·1,357 words·Part II — The Practice

Oral and manual sex are the most versatile skills in the bedroom. They do not depend on stamina, erection, or a particular body position. They can be the whole encounter or part of a larger one. They are also the areas where many people receive the least guidance and the most anxiety.

This chapter is about principles, not choreography. The specifics will vary with your partner, but the foundations are consistent: consent, communication, cleanliness, lubrication, pressure, rhythm, and attention.

Before you begin #

Consent and check-ins #

Ask before touching someone's genitals with your mouth or hands, especially with a new partner. "Can I go down on you?" or "Do you want my hands here?" is direct, respectful, and surprisingly sexy.

Check in during, too. "More pressure?" "Slower?" "Do you want me to keep going?" These questions are not interruptions. They are part of the experience.

Hygiene #

Basic hygiene is not optional:

  • Wash your hands and trim your nails. Rough nails can cause microscopic tears and discomfort.
  • Shower if you have been sweating or if it has been a while.
  • Clean toys before and after use.
  • Do not use scented products, douches, or harsh soaps on sensitive areas. They can disrupt the natural balance and cause irritation.

Barriers and protection #

Barriers reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections and make some people feel more comfortable.

  • Condoms for oral sex on a penis. Flavored condoms are available, though some people dislike the taste.
  • Dental dams or cut-open condoms for oral sex on a vulva or anus. These are less common but useful.
  • Gloves for manual sex, especially if you have cuts, hangnails, or are exploring the anus. Nitrile gloves are a good option.
  • Condoms on toys when sharing, and a fresh condom when moving from one partner or one orifice to another.

Barriers are not an insult. They are care. If a partner resists using one, that is a conversation about safety, not a negotiation about your worth.

Lubrication #

Lubricant makes everything better. It reduces friction, improves sensation, and makes sex more comfortable — especially for people with vulvas, people who are nervous, and people using condoms.

  • Water-based lubricant is compatible with condoms and silicone toys. It absorbs quickly, so you may need to reapply.
  • Silicone-based lubricant lasts longer and is good for shower sex, but it can damage silicone toys.
  • Oil-based lubricant is not compatible with latex condoms and can be difficult to clean up.
  • Saliva is not a reliable lubricant. It dries quickly and carries bacteria.

Apply lubricant generously. More is usually better than less. If something feels dry or sticky, add more.

Watch out · Numbing products

Avoid numbing lubricants or desensitizing products unless a clinician recommends them. Pain is information. Numbing it can lead to injury and does not address the cause.

Giving pleasure with your hands #

Hands are underrated. They are precise, versatile, and not limited by stamina. A good hand technique is not about speed; it is about pressure, rhythm, and attention.

External clitoral stimulation #

The clitoris is the most reliable route to orgasm for most people with vulvas. The visible glans is highly sensitive, but it can also be too sensitive for direct, dry contact. Start indirect and adjust.

Principles:

  • Start around the clitoris, not on it. Use the labia, the mons, or the area around the glans.
  • Use lubrication. Dry friction is uncomfortable for most people.
  • Ask about pressure. Some people want feather-light touch; others want firm, consistent pressure. Do not assume.
  • Keep a rhythm. Once you find something that works, stay with it. Changing rhythm constantly can prevent orgasm.
  • Do not stop too soon. If your partner is close, keep doing what you are doing. Ask before changing anything.
  • Combine with other touch. Kissing, breast stimulation, or internal stimulation can enhance pleasure.

Internal stimulation #

Internal stimulation can be pleasurable, but it is not automatically better than external stimulation. For many people, it works best in combination with clitoral stimulation.

Principles:

  • Start slow. Use one finger, plenty of lubricant, and a gentle approach.
  • Follow comfort. If your partner tenses or says it hurts, stop or adjust.
  • Explore the front wall. The area sometimes called the G-spot is part of the CUV complex. It may feel sensitive, or it may not. Use a gentle "come here" motion if your partner enjoys it.
  • Do not hunt for a magic spot. Exploration is fine; obsession is not. Ask what feels good.
  • Combine with external stimulation. Many people need clitoral stimulation to orgasm, even with internal stimulation.

Anal stimulation #

Anal play requires explicit consent, relaxation, hygiene, and lots of lubricant. It is not for everyone, and that is fine.

If you explore it:

  • Ask first. Do not surprise your partner.
  • Start external. Gentle touch around the anus can be pleasurable for some people.
  • Use gloves and lubricant. The tissue is delicate.
  • Go slowly. Relaxation is essential. Stop if there is pain.
  • Never move from the anus to the vagina or mouth without changing condoms or washing thoroughly. This is a basic hygiene rule.
  • Communicate constantly. Anal play requires more check-ins, not fewer.

Giving pleasure with your mouth #

Oral sex is intimate, versatile, and often deeply appreciated. It is also an area where confidence matters more than technique.

Oral sex on a vulva #

Principles:

  • Start slow. Kiss the inner thighs, the mons, and the labia before going to the clitoris.
  • Use your hands. Spread the labia gently, hold the clitoral hood back, or stimulate internally while your mouth works.
  • Mind the pressure. The clitoris can be very sensitive. Start with broad, flat tongue pressure rather than a pointed, direct attack.
  • Be consistent. Once you find a rhythm your partner likes, keep it. Do not switch techniques every few seconds.
  • Use lubrication. A little lubricant can make oral sex more comfortable, as long as it is safe to ingest (water-based is usually fine).
  • Breathe through your nose. It helps you maintain rhythm and avoid getting lightheaded.
  • Do not ignore feedback. If your partner says "softer" or "right there," adjust immediately.

Common mistakes: rushing, too much direct pressure too soon, teeth, inconsistency, and treating it as a race to orgasm.

Oral sex on a penis #

Principles:

  • Ask about pressure and pace. Some people prefer a firm grip and fast rhythm; others prefer slow and gentle.
  • Use your hands. Combine your mouth with a hand to control depth and pressure.
  • Watch the teeth. Cover your teeth with your lips, especially if you are new to it.
  • Mind the gag reflex. You do not have to take someone deep to give pleasure. Use your hands and mouth together.
  • Pay attention to the whole area. The glans, shaft, scrotum, and perineum can all be sensitive.
  • Communicate. "Do you like this?" "Faster?" "More pressure?"

Common mistakes: going too fast, ignoring feedback, using teeth, and treating depth as the goal.

Oral sex on the anus #

Anilingus requires explicit consent, thorough hygiene, and barrier protection. It is not for everyone. If you explore it, use a dental dam or cut-open condom, start slowly, and communicate constantly.

Receiving pleasure #

Giving is only half the equation. If you are on the receiving end, your job is to communicate.

  • Say what feels good. "Right there." "A little softer." "Keep doing that."
  • Guide with your hands. Move your partner's hand or head gently.
  • Do not fake. Moaning or pretending to enjoy something to manage your partner's ego makes it harder for them to learn what you actually like.
  • Give feedback after. "I loved it when you did X" is useful information.
  • Be patient with yourself. Receiving pleasure can be vulnerable, especially if you are used to performing.

Tip · The consistency principle

Once you find something your partner likes, keep doing it. Many people lose orgasms because their partner changes technique at the worst possible moment. Consistency is often more valuable than creativity.

The takeaway #

Oral and manual sex are skills built on attention, communication, and care. There is no universal technique, but there are universal principles: ask, start slow, use lubrication, pay attention, and adjust. The best lovers are not the ones with the most moves. They are the ones who make their partner feel safe enough to say what they want.

Penetration, Rhythm, and Variety

How to make penetration part of a larger pleasure picture — and why rhythm matters more than acrobatics.

6 min read·1,264 words·Part II — The Practice

Penetration gets more cultural attention than any other sex act. It is the implied climax of most movies, the default definition of "going all the way," and the act around which many people organize their entire sexual self-image. That is a lot of weight to put on one activity.

This chapter is not anti-penetration. It is anti-penetration-only. Penetration can be intimate, intense, and deeply pleasurable. It is also one option among many, and it works best when it is part of a larger picture that includes arousal, communication, clitoral stimulation, and comfort.

Before penetration #

Arousal and lubrication #

Penetration is more comfortable and more pleasurable when the body is aroused. Arousal increases blood flow, lubrication, and elasticity. It also changes the angle and sensation of the vaginal canal.

Do not use penetration as a test of arousal. If your partner is not lubricated or relaxed, that is not a verdict on your attractiveness or their desire. It is information: slow down, add lubricant, spend more time on foreplay, or choose a different activity.

Use lubricant generously. Even when natural lubrication is present, added lubricant can improve comfort and sensation. Water-based lubricant is a good default; silicone-based lubricant lasts longer but can damage silicone toys.

Consent and comfort #

Ask before penetration, especially with a new partner. "Do you want me inside you?" or "Are you ready for more?" is direct and respectful.

Check in during. "Does this feel good?" "Deeper or shallower?" "Do you want to change position?" Penetration can become uncomfortable quickly, and small adjustments make a big difference.

Contraception and protection #

If pregnancy is a possibility, use contraception. If STI protection is relevant, use condoms or another barrier method. Discuss these before sex, not in the moment.

Condoms are not a mood killer. They are a basic form of care. If a partner refuses to use one, that is a boundary conversation, not a persuasion challenge.

Rhythm #

Rhythm is the difference between penetration that feels mechanical and penetration that feels alive. It is also the thing most people get wrong.

Start slow #

A common mistake is to start at full speed. This is often uncomfortable and rarely pleasurable. Start slow, shallow, and gentle. Let your partner's body adjust. Pay attention to their breath, their hips, and their sounds.

Build gradually #

Once you are both comfortable, gradually increase speed or depth. Do not jump from zero to maximum. Build in increments, checking in as you go.

Consistency matters #

Once you find a rhythm your partner likes, stay with it. Many people lose orgasms because their partner changes speed or angle at the worst possible moment. If your partner says "keep doing that," do exactly that. Do not get creative.

Vary deliberately #

Variation is useful when it is intentional, not constant. Try:

  • Slow, deep strokes followed by faster, shallower ones.
  • A pause at the deepest point.
  • A grinding motion rather than an in-and-out motion.
  • A change of angle rather than a change of speed.
  • A pause to kiss, breathe, or check in.

The key is to vary one thing at a time and notice the response.

Tip · The pause

When you feel yourself rushing toward orgasm, pause. Stop moving. Breathe. Kiss your partner. Then resume. The pause is not a failure; it is a technique. It can also be intensely erotic.

Angles and positions #

There is no universal "best" position. The best position is the one that is comfortable, consensual, and pleasurable for both people. That said, small changes in angle can make a big difference.

Missionary #

Missionary is underrated. It allows eye contact, kissing, clitoral stimulation, and a range of angles.

  • Pillow under the hips. This can change the angle of penetration and make certain positions more comfortable.
  • Legs on shoulders. This can allow deeper penetration, but it is not comfortable for everyone. Ask first.
  • Grinding rather than thrusting. A slow, grinding motion can provide clitoral stimulation and a different sensation.
  • Hands free. Use one hand to stimulate the clitoris, hold hands, or touch your partner's body.

Cowgirl / rider #

This position gives the receiving partner more control over depth, angle, and rhythm. It can be empowering and pleasurable, but it can also be tiring. Support your partner's weight if needed, and check in.

Doggy style #

This position allows deep penetration and a different angle. It can be intense, but it can also be uncomfortable if the angle is wrong. Use pillows to adjust height, and check in frequently. Some people find it impersonal; others find it exciting. Ask.

Side-by-side #

Side-by-side positions are often more comfortable and allow close body contact, kissing, and clitoral stimulation. They are good for slower, more intimate sex and for people who find other positions tiring.

Standing #

Standing positions can be passionate but are often physically demanding and dependent on height differences. They are not a requirement. If they do not work, laugh and try something else.

Oral and manual positions #

Penetration is not the only position-based pleasure. Oral and manual sex can be done in many positions, and they are often more reliable for orgasm than penetration alone.

Clitoral stimulation during penetration #

For many people with vulvas, penetration alone is not enough for orgasm. Combining penetration with clitoral stimulation — with a hand, a toy, or a pillow — can make a significant difference.

Options:

  • Your hand. Reach around or use a free hand to stimulate the clitoris.
  • Their hand. Ask your partner to touch themselves while you are inside them. Many people find this easier and more effective.
  • A toy. A small vibrator or clitoral stimulator can be used during penetration. Ask first, and make sure it is comfortable.
  • Grinding. A position that presses the vulva against your body or a pillow can provide indirect clitoral stimulation.

Do not assume that penetration should be the sole source of pleasure. Treat clitoral stimulation as part of the experience, not a consolation prize.

Pain and discomfort #

Pain during penetration is common, but it is not something to push through. It can have many causes: lack of arousal, lack of lubrication, infection, pelvic-floor tension, endometriosis, vaginal dryness, scar tissue, or a mismatch in angle or depth.

If penetration hurts:

  • Stop. Do not grit your teeth and endure it.
  • Add lubricant. Dryness is a common cause.
  • Change angle or depth. Sometimes a small adjustment helps.
  • Slow down. Relaxation takes time.
  • Talk about it. "It hurts when you go deep" is useful information.
  • See a healthcare provider if it persists. Pain is treatable, and you deserve proper care.

Watch out · Do not normalize pain

Sex should not hurt. Discomfort is a signal to adjust, not a challenge to overcome. If a partner says it hurts, stop immediately and change course. If they say it always hurts, encourage them to see a clinician.

Variety without acrobatics #

Variety does not require a circus. Small changes can keep sex interesting:

  • A different room, time of day, or lighting.
  • A new position, or a variation on a familiar one.
  • A toy, a blindfold, or a massage oil — with consent.
  • A change in pace, from slow and tender to playful and energetic.
  • A longer build-up, or a shorter, more urgent encounter.
  • Talking about a fantasy, or sharing a desire.

Variety is not about novelty for its own sake. It is about staying curious and responsive.

The takeaway #

Penetration is one part of sex, not the whole thing. It works best when it is built on arousal, communication, comfort, and clitoral stimulation. Rhythm matters more than acrobatics. Consistency matters more than creativity. And the best position is the one that feels good to the people involved — not the one that looks impressive.

Lasting Longer: Breath, Edging, and Pelvic Floor

Evidence-informed ways to build control, reduce anxiety, and change the finish line — without turning sex into a training drill.

7 min read·1,529 words·Part II — The Practice

If you finish sooner than you want, you are in good company. Premature ejaculation is one of the most common sexual concerns among people with penises. It is also one of the most treatable. The problem is that most people never get good information about it, so they rely on distraction, gritted teeth, or shame.

This chapter covers the practical side of lasting longer: breathing, pacing, stop-start, edging, pelvic-floor training, and when to seek professional help. It also covers the mindset that makes those techniques work — because control is not just a physical skill.

What "lasting longer" actually means #

There is no universal correct duration. The average time to ejaculation during penetrative sex is often cited as around five to seven minutes, but that number varies widely and is not a standard anyone needs to meet.

Clinically, premature ejaculation is usually described as ejaculation that:

  • Happens sooner than the person wants, consistently.
  • Causes distress or avoidance.
  • Occurs within about one minute of penetration (lifelong PE) or represents a significant reduction from previous latency (acquired PE).

The key word is distress. If you and your partner are happy with your sex life, you do not have a problem to fix. If you are distressed, there are things you can do.

Note · Not a masculinity test

Lasting longer is not a measure of manhood. It is a skill, and like any skill, it depends on physiology, practice, anxiety, and context. Shame makes it worse. Information makes it better.

Why it happens #

Premature ejaculation can have several contributors:

  • Anxiety and performance pressure. Worry activates the sympathetic nervous system and speeds up the reflex.
  • Sensitivity. Some people are simply more sensitive to stimulation.
  • Conditioning. If you learned to rush solo sex to avoid being caught, your body may have learned to finish quickly.
  • Relationship stress. Conflict, pressure, or fear of judgment can affect control.
  • Novelty or excitement. A new partner or situation can increase arousal.
  • Pelvic-floor tension. A tight or uncoordinated pelvic floor can contribute.
  • Medical factors. Prostatitis, thyroid issues, and some medications can play a role.

Often it is a combination. That is why a single technique rarely solves it on its own.

Start with the mind #

Before you try any physical technique, address the pressure.

  • Stop treating sex as a countdown. The goal is not a number. The goal is pleasure.
  • Tell your partner. "I sometimes finish faster than I want. I'm working on it, and I'd like to slow down." Honesty reduces anxiety.
  • Take penetration off the pedestal. If you finish early, you still have hands, a mouth, toys, and time. Sex is not over.
  • Do not apologize repeatedly. One acknowledgment is enough. Excessive apology makes your partner responsible for managing your shame.
  • Focus on sensation, not monitoring. The more you watch the clock, the worse it gets.

Breathing #

Breathing is the simplest and most accessible tool.

When you are highly aroused, your breathing becomes shallow and fast. Slow, deep breathing activates the parasympathetic nervous system — the "rest and digest" branch — which helps counteract the urgency.

Try this:

  1. Breathe into your belly, not your chest.
  2. Inhale for four counts, exhale for six.
  3. Keep your shoulders relaxed.
  4. Use the breath as a pause, not a distraction. You are not trying to leave your body; you are trying to stay in it without rushing.

You can practice breathing outside sex, then use it during sex when you feel yourself approaching the point of no return.

Stop-start #

The stop-start method (sometimes called the Semans technique) is one of the most established behavioral approaches.

How it works:

  1. Begin sex or masturbation as usual.
  2. When you feel yourself approaching the point of no return, stop all stimulation.
  3. Wait 10–30 seconds, or until the sensation subsides.
  4. Resume when you feel ready.
  5. Repeat as needed.

You can practice alone first, then with a partner. With a partner, tell them what you are doing so they do not interpret the pause as rejection or disinterest. "I'm pausing to cool down. Give me a second" is enough.

The goal is not to never approach the edge. The goal is to learn that you can approach it, pause, and return — and that the pause is not a failure.

Edging #

Edging is a solo practice that builds awareness and control. It involves bringing yourself close to orgasm, then stopping or slowing down, repeatedly, before finally allowing release.

A simple routine:

  • Spend 10–15 minutes cycling between high arousal and a lower plateau.
  • Stop before you reach the point of no return.
  • Breathe, relax your pelvic floor, and wait until the urgency drops.
  • Repeat two or three times before finishing.

Edging is not a test of willpower. If you go over the edge, that is fine. The point is to learn the signals leading up to it.

Watch out · Do not overdo it

Excessive edging or edging with intense pressure can cause pelvic-floor tension or discomfort. Keep sessions moderate, and stop if you feel pain or lingering tension.

The squeeze technique #

The squeeze technique is a variation of stop-start. When you feel close to orgasm, stop stimulation and apply gentle pressure to the head of the penis (or just below it) for a few seconds. This can reduce the urge to ejaculate.

Use light pressure, not pain. If it hurts, stop. The squeeze technique is best learned alone before trying it with a partner.

Position and pace changes #

Sometimes the simplest solution is to change what you are doing.

  • Slow down. Reduce speed and depth.
  • Change position. A less stimulating position can buy time.
  • Pause at the deepest point. Stop thrusting and breathe.
  • Use shallower strokes. Deep penetration is often more stimulating.
  • Shift focus. Give your partner oral or manual pleasure for a while.
  • Use a condom. Condoms can reduce sensitivity for some people.
  • Try a thicker condom or a desensitizing lubricant — but only with clinician guidance, and never without your partner's knowledge.

Pelvic-floor training #

The pelvic floor plays a role in ejaculation and erection. A stronger, more coordinated pelvic floor can improve control — but more is not always better. A tight, overactive pelvic floor can cause problems too.

Finding the muscles #

Imagine you are stopping the flow of urine midstream or holding in gas. You should feel a lift and squeeze around the base of the penis and the anus. Do not clench your abs, thighs, or buttocks.

Do not routinely stop urine flow as an exercise. Use it only to identify the muscles once or twice. Stopping urine regularly can disrupt bladder function.

A basic routine #

  • Squeeze and lift for 3–5 seconds.
  • Fully relax for the same amount of time.
  • Repeat 8–12 times per set.
  • Do 2–3 sets per day.
  • Progress to 8–10 second holds as you get stronger.
  • Add quick pulses — short squeezes — after the slow holds.

Consistency matters more than intensity. Do not hold your breath. Do not clench constantly. Full relaxation is as important as the squeeze.

Using the muscles during sex #

Once you can isolate the muscles, you can use a gentle squeeze to help manage arousal. Do not clamp down hard. A light, controlled lift can help you pause and reset.

If you cannot feel the muscles, or if you have pelvic pain, see a pelvic-floor physical therapist. They can assess your technique and rule out problems.

Biofeedback #

Biofeedback is a professional technique that uses sensors to show you what your pelvic floor is doing in real time. It can be helpful if you are not sure you are activating the right muscles, or if you are not progressing with home exercises.

A typical course involves an assessment, sensor placement, guided practice, and a home program. It is generally safe and often effective, especially when combined with behavioral techniques. Ask your clinician whether it is appropriate for you.

When to see a professional #

Consider talking to a doctor or sex therapist if:

  • Premature ejaculation is causing significant distress or avoidance.
  • You have tried self-help techniques for several months without improvement.
  • You have pain, urinary symptoms, or other medical concerns.
  • You have difficulty getting or maintaining an erection.
  • You experience delayed ejaculation or no ejaculation.
  • You feel anxious or depressed about sex.

Treatment options may include behavioral therapy, couples therapy, pelvic-floor physical therapy, topical anesthetics, or medication. These are legitimate medical options, not admissions of failure.

Delayed ejaculation #

At the other end of the spectrum is delayed ejaculation — difficulty reaching orgasm despite adequate stimulation and arousal. It can be frustrating for both partners.

Possible causes include:

  • Medication side effects (especially some antidepressants).
  • Anxiety or performance pressure.
  • Relationship issues.
  • Excessive masturbation with a specific technique or grip.
  • Nerve or hormonal issues.
  • Alcohol or drug use.

If you are experiencing delayed ejaculation, do not assume it is permanent. Talk to a clinician, review your medications, and consider sex therapy. It is treatable.

The takeaway #

Lasting longer is a skill, not a verdict on your masculinity. The most effective approach combines relaxation, communication, behavioral techniques, pelvic-floor training, and — when needed — professional support. Do not try to white-knuckle your way through it. Learn your body, ask for help, and remember that sex is bigger than one reflex.

Aftercare and Feedback

The minutes after sex shape how the whole experience is remembered — and how good the next one will be.

4 min read·976 words·Part II — The Practice

Most advice about sex focuses on the middle. Very little focuses on the beginning of the conversation or the minutes after. That is a mistake. Aftercare — the care you give each other after sex — is part of sex, and it has a disproportionate effect on how the experience is remembered.

Aftercare is not just for intense or kinky sex, and it is not just for one partner. Everyone can benefit from it. It is also one of the easiest ways to build trust, improve communication, and make future sex better.

What aftercare is #

Aftercare is the physical and emotional care that follows sex. It can include:

  • Physical comfort: water, a blanket, a snack, a shower, a warm room.
  • Close contact: cuddling, holding, stroking, lying together.
  • Verbal affirmation: "That was lovely." "I'm glad we did that." "I love being close to you."
  • Check-in: "Are you okay?" "How are you feeling?" "Was there anything you didn't like?"
  • Space: some people need quiet, solitude, or time to themselves. That is valid too.

Aftercare is not a fixed script. It is whatever helps each person feel safe, cared for, and connected after vulnerability.

Why it matters #

Sex can be emotionally intense. It involves exposure — physical, emotional, and sometimes social. The moments after sex are when people are most open and most fragile. How you treat each other then can reinforce trust or undermine it.

Aftercare also helps with:

  • Emotional regulation. Oxytocin and other hormones can make people feel sleepy, tearful, clingy, or withdrawn. Aftercare gives those feelings a safe place to land.
  • Repair. If something awkward or uncomfortable happened, aftercare is the time to check in and reconnect.
  • Feedback. It is easier to talk about what worked and what did not when you are calm and close.
  • Anticipation. People who feel cared for after sex are more likely to want sex again. Aftercare is not just kindness; it is good relationship maintenance.

Note · Not everyone wants cuddling

Some people feel touched-out, overstimulated, or simply need space after sex. Do not assume that your preferred aftercare is your partner's. Ask. "Do you want to cuddle, or would you like some space?" is a caring question.

The aftercare check-in #

A simple aftercare check-in can be short:

  1. Physical: "Do you need water, a blanket, a shower, anything?"
  2. Emotional: "How are you feeling?"
  3. Experience: "Was there anything you loved? Anything you didn't?"
  4. Connection: "I'm glad we did that." "I like being close to you."

Keep it light unless your partner wants to go deeper. The goal is not to conduct a formal review. The goal is to make sure everyone feels okay.

The debrief #

A debrief is a slightly more structured conversation, ideally the next day or after a pause. It is not a performance review. It is a chance to learn.

Questions that work:

  • "What did you enjoy most?"
  • "Was there anything you wanted more of?"
  • "Was there anything you didn't like, or want to do differently next time?"
  • "Is there anything you've been curious about?"
  • "How did you feel afterward?"

Questions that do not work:

  • "Was I good?"
  • "Did you come?"
  • "Why didn't you do X?"
  • "Was I better than your ex?"

The first set invites information. The second set invites defensiveness.

Giving feedback #

Use the same principles as Chapter 2: be specific, timely, and kind.

  • "I loved it when you did X."
  • "I'd like to try Y next time."
  • "A little more pressure felt amazing."
  • "I wasn't sure about Z, but I'm glad we tried it."

Avoid global judgments: "You always..." or "You never..." They turn a preference into a character flaw.

Receiving feedback #

  • Listen.
  • Thank your partner.
  • Ask for clarification.
  • Do not argue with their experience. If they say something felt a certain way, that is their experience. You can explain your intention later, but first make room for their account.
  • Follow up. "Was that better?" shows you care.

Rejection and repair #

Not every initiation will be welcomed. Not every encounter will go well. Sometimes one person is tired, stressed, or simply not in the mood. Sometimes something awkward happens.

Rejection is not a verdict on your worth. It is information about the moment. A good response is:

  • "That's okay. Thanks for telling me."
  • "No problem. Do you want to just cuddle?"
  • "I'm disappointed, but I'm glad you said no instead of going along with it."

Repair after an awkward moment:

  • "I'm sorry. I moved too fast."
  • "I didn't mean to make you uncomfortable."
  • "Can we talk about what happened?"
  • "What do you need right now?"

Repair is not about being perfect. It is about being accountable and reconnecting.

Aftercare after casual sex #

Aftercare is not only for relationships. If you have sex with a casual partner, check in, offer water, make sure they get home safely, and respect their boundaries. You do not have to cuddle for an hour, but you should not disappear the moment you are done.

A simple "Are you okay? Do you need anything?" is enough. If you are the one leaving, say goodbye properly. If you are the one staying, make sure your partner knows they are welcome to leave or stay.

The next day #

Aftercare can extend beyond the immediate aftermath. A text the next day — "I had a lovely time. Hope you're well" — can mean a lot. It signals that you see the person, not just the experience.

If something felt off, the next day is often a better time to talk about it. "I've been thinking about last night. I wanted to check in about X" is a gentle opener.

The takeaway #

Aftercare is not an optional extra. It is part of sex. It is how you tell your partner, in words and actions, that they matter beyond the orgasm. It is also how you learn, repair, and build a sex life that gets better over time.
