Health, Habits, and Keeping It Good

The everyday habits, health decisions, and relationship practices that shape desire over the long term.

5 min read·1,191 words·Part III — The Long Game

Good sex is not just a bedroom skill. It is downstream of sleep, stress, health, self-image, and the quality of your relationships. You can learn every technique in this book and still struggle if you are exhausted, anxious, disconnected, or unwell.

This chapter is about the long game: the habits that support desire, the health issues that deserve attention, and the relationship practices that keep sex interesting over years rather than weeks.

The body is a system #

Sexual function depends on the whole body. Cardiovascular health affects blood flow. Sleep affects hormones and mood. Stress affects arousal. Medication can affect desire, erection, and orgasm. Mental health affects everything.

That means "sexual problems" are sometimes not sexual at all. They are signals that something else needs attention.

Sleep #

Chronic sleep deprivation lowers testosterone, increases stress hormones, and reduces energy and mood. It also makes people irritable and less patient — not a great combination for intimacy.

Aim for seven to nine hours if you can. Keep a consistent sleep schedule. Treat sleep as part of your sex life, not a separate category.

Exercise #

Regular movement improves blood flow, stamina, mood, and body confidence. It does not have to be extreme. Walking, strength training, yoga, cycling, swimming — anything you enjoy and can sustain.

Cardiovascular health matters for erection and arousal. Strength training supports pelvic-floor function and overall energy. Exercise is not a punishment for your body; it is care for it.

Nutrition #

There is no magic food that makes you better in bed. A balanced diet supports energy, mood, and vascular health. Extreme diets, disordered eating, and body obsession can harm desire and self-image.

If you have a complicated relationship with food or your body, consider talking to a professional. Body image and sexual pleasure are closely linked.

Alcohol and drugs #

A drink can lower inhibitions, but alcohol also impairs arousal, erection, orgasm, and judgment. Heavy or habitual drinking can reduce desire and make consent impossible.

Cannabis and other drugs affect people differently. Some people find them relaxing; others find them anxiety-provoking or disorienting. If you use them, know your limits, and never pressure a partner to use them.

Smoking and vaping #

Smoking damages blood vessels and reduces circulation, which can affect erection and arousal. Vaping is not harmless. If you smoke, quitting is one of the best things you can do for your sexual health.

Medications #

Some medications — including certain antidepressants, blood-pressure drugs, and hormonal treatments — can affect desire, erection, arousal, or orgasm. Do not stop taking a prescribed medication without talking to your doctor. Ask about alternatives and side effects.

Mental health #

Anxiety, depression, trauma, and stress can all affect sex. So can the medication used to treat them. This is not a personal failing. It is a health issue, and it is treatable.

Therapy can help with:

  • Performance anxiety.
  • Body image.
  • Trauma and consent.
  • Relationship conflict.
  • Low desire.
  • Compulsive sexual behavior.
  • Shame.

If you are struggling, reach out. A good therapist will not judge you.

Sexual health care #

STI testing #

Regular testing is part of responsible sex. Many STIs are asymptomatic, so you cannot tell by looking. Testing is quick, often free or low-cost, and confidential.

Talk to your partners about testing. "When were you last tested?" is a normal question, not an accusation. If you have an STI, disclose it before sex and follow treatment advice.

Contraception #

If pregnancy is a possibility, choose a method that works for you and discuss it before sex. Options include condoms, hormonal methods, IUDs, implants, diaphragms, and sterilization. No method is perfect, and some methods have side effects. A clinician can help you choose.

Vaccination #

HPV vaccination reduces the risk of genital warts and several cancers. Hepatitis B vaccination is also relevant to sexual health. Ask your clinician whether you are up to date.

Pelvic health #

Pelvic-floor issues — pain, tension, weakness, incontinence — are common and treatable. Do not accept pain during sex as normal. A pelvic-floor physical therapist can help.

Desire over the long term #

Long-term desire is not a constant flame. It fluctuates with stress, health, hormones, relationship dynamics, and life. That is normal. The mistake is assuming that a drop in desire means the relationship is doomed or that you are broken.

Spontaneous vs. responsive desire #

Some people feel desire spontaneously: they think about sex and want it. Others feel desire responsively: they become interested after arousal begins, after relaxation, or after connection. Neither is better. If you have responsive desire, waiting to feel spontaneous desire before initiating can leave you waiting forever. Sometimes you have to start and see what happens.

Novelty and familiarity #

Novelty can boost desire, but so can safety and familiarity. The key is to avoid both stagnation and chaos. Try new things, but not so many that you never relax into what you know.

Ideas:

  • A regular date night that is not about sex, but often leads there.
  • A new activity together — dancing, hiking, a class.
  • A conversation about fantasies, without pressure to act on them.
  • A change of scenery: a hotel, a weekend away, a different room.
  • A shared project that builds teamwork and connection.

Scheduling sex #

Scheduling sounds unromantic. It is also one of the most effective things long-term couples do. Desire is not always spontaneous; making time for sex increases the chances that it will happen.

A scheduled encounter does not have to be rigid. It can be a window: "Thursday night is ours." If it does not happen, that is okay. The point is to prioritize intimacy rather than waiting for the perfect mood.

Intimacy outside sex #

Sex is not the only form of intimacy. Hugging, kissing, holding hands, talking, laughing, and simply being together all build the connection that makes sex better. If the only time you touch is when you want sex, touch becomes a negotiation. If touch is part of everyday life, sex becomes an extension of closeness rather than a demand.

Aging, disability, and chronic illness #

Sex does not end at a certain age, and it does not require a perfect body. Aging, disability, chronic illness, surgery, and medication can change how sex works, but they do not eliminate the need for intimacy and pleasure.

Adaptation is possible:

  • Different positions and aids.
  • More emphasis on touch, oral, and manual pleasure.
  • Communication about energy, pain, and timing.
  • Medical support for symptoms.
  • A broader definition of sex that does not center penetration.

If you or your partner are navigating health changes, talk to a clinician who understands sexual health. You deserve pleasure at every stage of life.

Key idea · The long game

The habits that make good sex possible are the same habits that make a good life possible: sleep, movement, honest communication, care, and curiosity. There is no separate sex self. There is just you, in a body, with another person.

The takeaway #

Sexual health is health. Sleep, exercise, stress, medication, mental health, and relationship quality all shape desire and pleasure. Attend to the basics, get help when you need it, and do not treat fluctuations in desire as failures. The long game is not about maintaining a perfect sex life. It is about staying curious, connected, and willing to adapt.

Communication Scripts and Checklists

Ready-to-use phrases, checklists, and conversation starters for before, during, and after sex.

3 min read·760 words·Appendices

The hardest part of communication is often finding the first sentence. These scripts are starting points, not lines to recite. Adapt them to your voice, your relationship, and the moment.

Consent scripts #

Before sex #

  • "I'd really like to kiss you. Is that okay?"
  • "I'm interested in taking this further. How are you feeling about that?"
  • "What are you comfortable with tonight?"
  • "I want to try something. Want to hear it first?"
  • "Do you want to keep going, or would you rather slow down?"

During sex #

  • "Is this okay?"
  • "Do you want more of this?"
  • "Harder or softer?"
  • "Right there?"
  • "Do you want me to keep going?"
  • "I need to pause for a second. Is that okay?"

When you want to stop #

  • "I need to stop. Can we pause?"
  • "I'm not comfortable with this anymore."
  • "I'm not feeling it tonight. Can we just cuddle?"
  • "That's a no for me. I'm still happy to be here with you."

When your partner wants to stop #

  • "Of course. Thank you for telling me."
  • "Do you need anything? Water, a blanket, some space?"
  • "I'm glad you said something. Let's take care of you."

Tip · The simplest check-in

When in doubt, ask: "What do you want right now?" It is open, respectful, and gives your partner room to answer honestly.

Feedback scripts #

Giving positive feedback #

  • "I love it when you do that."
  • "That feels amazing. Keep going."
  • "I like a little more pressure."
  • "Slower feels really good."
  • "I want to try X. Would you be into that?"

Giving difficult feedback #

  • "I want to tell you something, and I want you to know it's not a criticism of you."
  • "I liked X, but Y was a little uncomfortable. Could we try Z instead?"
  • "I need a little more warm-up before we go there."
  • "I'm feeling a bit anxious. Can we slow down?"

Receiving feedback #

  • "Thank you for telling me."
  • "Can you show me what you mean?"
  • "I hear you. Let me try that."
  • "I'm sorry that felt bad. What would feel better?"

Conversation starters #

For a new partner #

  • "What do you enjoy?"
  • "What's off the table for you?"
  • "How do you like to be touched?"
  • "What makes you feel safe?"
  • "How will we tell each other if we want to stop?"

For a long-term partner #

  • "What's something you've been wanting more of?"
  • "Is there anything you'd like to try that we haven't done?"
  • "What makes you feel most desired?"
  • "When do you feel closest to me?"
  • "Is there anything I do that doesn't work for you?"

After sex #

  • "What did you enjoy most?"
  • "Was there anything you wanted more of?"
  • "How are you feeling?"
  • "I loved being close to you."
  • "Is there anything you need right now?"

Pre-sex checklist #

  • We have both consented enthusiastically and specifically.
  • We have discussed boundaries and what is off the table.
  • We have contraception and STI protection if relevant.
  • We have lubricant.
  • Hands are clean, nails are trimmed.
  • Toys are clean and condoms are available if needed.
  • We have privacy and enough time.
  • We know how to signal stop or pause.
  • We are both sober enough to consent clearly.

Aftercare checklist #

  • Water or a drink nearby.
  • A blanket or something warm.
  • A check-in: "How are you feeling?"
  • Physical comfort: cuddling, holding, or space, depending on preference.
  • A word of affirmation: "I'm glad we did that."
  • A bathroom break if needed.
  • A conversation about anything that felt off, if both people are ready.
  • A plan for the next day, if relevant.

A five-minute debrief #

Use this after a pause, or the next day:

  1. One thing I loved: "I loved it when..."
  2. One thing I'd like more of: "Next time, I'd like..."
  3. One thing I'd like to try: "I'm curious about..."
  4. One thing I need: "I need..."
  5. One thing I appreciate about you: "I appreciate..."

Keep it short. The goal is connection and information, not a performance review.

Phrases to avoid #

  • "You always..." / "You never..." — global judgments invite defensiveness.
  • "Was I good?" — puts your partner in the position of grading you.
  • "Why didn't you...?" — sounds accusatory, even when it is not meant to be.
  • "Everyone else likes this." — comparison is not consent or evidence.
  • "If you loved me, you would..." — pressure is not consent.

A note on awkwardness #

You will not always say the right thing. You will sometimes ask a question at the wrong moment, laugh at the wrong time, or misread a signal. That is normal. Repair is more important than perfection. "I'm sorry, that came out wrong. Can we try that again?" is almost always enough.

B

Myths vs. Evidence

Ten common beliefs about sex that deserve a second look.

3 min read·718 words·Appendices

Myths about sex are passed around like folklore. They shape expectations, create anxiety, and make people feel abnormal when their experience does not match the story. Here are ten of the most common — and what the evidence and clinical experience actually suggest.

Myth 1: Penetration is the main event #

The myth: Sex is foreplay, then penetration, then orgasm. Everything else is a warm-up.

The reality: Penetration is one sex act among many. For most people with vulvas, clitoral stimulation is the most reliable route to orgasm. Oral, manual, toys, kissing, and whole-body touch are not consolation prizes; they are sex. Framing penetration as the main event creates pressure and leaves a lot of pleasure off the table.

Myth 2: Most women orgasm from penetration alone #

The myth: If you are good at penetration, your partner will orgasm.

The reality: Research consistently finds that only a minority of people with vulvas — often cited as around 18% — report that penetration alone is reliably sufficient for orgasm. Many need direct or indirect clitoral stimulation. This is not a technique failure; it is anatomy and variation.

Myth 3: The G-spot is a magic button #

The myth: There is a discrete spot on the front vaginal wall that reliably produces intense orgasms.

The reality: Anatomical studies have not consistently found a discrete G-spot. What many people feel is likely the CUV complex — the internal clitoris, urethra, and surrounding tissue. Some people find that area highly responsive; others do not. Exploration is fine. Obsession is not.

Myth 4: Size determines sexual satisfaction #

The myth: A larger penis means better sex.

The reality: Research on penis size and sexual satisfaction is mixed, but the effect is generally small compared with communication, technique, emotional connection, and clitoral stimulation. Many people report that skill and attentiveness matter more than size. Anxiety about size can interfere with pleasure more than size itself.

Myth 5: Good sex should be spontaneous #

The myth: Scheduling sex means the desire is gone.

The reality: Long-term desire fluctuates. Scheduling creates opportunities for intimacy and reduces the pressure to feel spontaneously ready. Many couples find that anticipation and planning increase desire rather than diminish it.

Myth 6: Men always want sex #

The myth: Men are always up for it; women are the ones who say no.

The reality: Desire varies by person, not by gender. Men can have low desire, responsive desire, or periods of not wanting sex. Women can have high desire and initiate frequently. Assuming a partner's desire based on gender leads to miscommunication and pressure.

Myth 7: Porn is a good guide to sex #

The myth: Porn shows what people want and how to do it.

The reality: Porn is entertainment. It is edited, staged, and optimized for visual impact, not for mutual pleasure. It often skips foreplay, ignores clitoral stimulation, and depicts endurance and positions that are not realistic or comfortable for most people. Use it as fantasy if you like; do not use it as an instruction manual.

Myth 8: If it hurts, you should push through #

The myth: Pain during sex is normal, especially the first time or with a new position.

The reality: Pain is a signal. It can have many causes — lack of arousal, lack of lubrication, infection, pelvic-floor tension, endometriosis, scar tissue, or a mismatch in angle. Stop, adjust, and see a clinician if it persists. Sex should not hurt.

Myth 9: Orgasms are the measure of good sex #

The myth: If no one orgasmed, the sex was a failure.

The reality: Orgasm is one possible outcome, not the definition of good sex. Many people have satisfying sex without orgasm; many have orgasms during sex that feels disconnected. Pleasure, connection, safety, and mutual care matter more than a scoreboard.

Myth 10: You should know what your partner wants without asking #

The myth: Asking ruins the mood; a good lover just knows.

The reality: Bodies and preferences are not standardized. Asking is not a sign of incompetence; it is a sign of attention. The best lovers are not mind readers. They are curious, responsive, and willing to learn.

Key idea · The pattern

Most sexual myths share the same flaw: they treat one body, one script, or one outcome as universal. Good sex is specific. It depends on the people involved, their communication, and their willingness to adapt.

A Simple Pelvic Floor Routine

A simple, safe routine for building pelvic-floor awareness and control — plus the mistakes to avoid.

3 min read·768 words·Appendices

The pelvic floor is a hammock of muscles that supports the bladder, bowel, and reproductive organs. It plays a role in erection, ejaculation, orgasm, continence, and core stability. Like any muscle group, it can be trained — but more is not always better. A tight, overactive pelvic floor can cause pain and dysfunction, so relaxation matters as much as strength.

This appendix is a general routine, not a personalized program. If you have pelvic pain, incontinence, recent surgery, or difficulty identifying the muscles, see a pelvic-floor physical therapist.

Step 1: Find the muscles #

Imagine you are stopping the flow of urine midstream or holding in gas. You should feel a gentle lift and squeeze around the base of the penis or the vagina and anus.

Do not clench your abs, thighs, or buttocks. Do not hold your breath. Do not routinely stop urine flow as an exercise; use it only once or twice to identify the muscles.

If you cannot feel the muscles, try:

  • Lying down with your knees bent.
  • Placing a hand on your lower belly to make sure it stays relaxed.
  • Using a mirror to see whether the perineum lifts.
  • Asking a pelvic-floor physical therapist for biofeedback.

Step 2: The basic routine #

Start with slow holds:

  • Squeeze and lift for 3–5 seconds.
  • Fully relax for the same amount of time.
  • Repeat 8–12 times per set.
  • Do 2–3 sets per day.

As you get stronger, progress to 8–10 second holds. Add quick pulses — short, gentle squeezes — after the slow holds.

Watch out · Relaxation is half the exercise

Many people focus only on squeezing. A pelvic floor that cannot relax is not a healthy pelvic floor. Spend at least as long relaxing as you do contracting. If you feel lingering tension, pain, or urgency, stop and consult a professional.

Step 3: Progress gradually #

Week 1–2:

  • 3–5 second holds.
  • 8 repetitions.
  • 2 sets per day.
  • Focus on technique, not strength.

Week 3–4:

  • 5–8 second holds.
  • 8–10 repetitions.
  • 2–3 sets per day.
  • Add 5–10 quick pulses at the end of each set.

Week 5–8:

  • 8–10 second holds.
  • 10–12 repetitions.
  • 3 sets per day.
  • Practice in different positions: lying, sitting, standing.

Do not add resistance, weights, or extreme repetition without professional guidance. More is not better if it creates tension or pain.

Step 4: Use the muscles during sex #

Once you can isolate the muscles, you can use a gentle squeeze to help manage arousal. Do not clamp down hard. A light, controlled lift can help you pause and reset.

For people with penises, a gentle squeeze near the point of high arousal can help delay ejaculation. For people with vulvas, pelvic-floor awareness can increase sensation and orgasm intensity. Start gently and notice what helps.

Step 5: Relax the pelvic floor #

Try a reverse Kegel:

  • Inhale slowly and imagine the pelvic floor softening and lengthening.
  • Do not push hard or strain.
  • Exhale gently.
  • Repeat 5–10 times.

You can also try diaphragmatic breathing: place a hand on your belly, breathe in so the belly expands, and let the pelvic floor relax on the inhale. This is especially useful if you tend to hold tension in your pelvis.

Common mistakes #

  • Clenching the abs, thighs, or buttocks instead of the pelvic floor.
  • Holding your breath.
  • Only squeezing, never relaxing.
  • Doing too many repetitions too soon.
  • Using the routine to "fix" pain without addressing the cause.
  • Stopping urine flow as a regular exercise.
  • Ignoring pain, urgency, or tension.

When to see a pelvic-floor physical therapist #

Consider professional help if:

  • You cannot identify the muscles.
  • You have pelvic pain or pain during sex.
  • You have incontinence or urgency.
  • You have recently had surgery or childbirth.
  • You are not progressing after several weeks.
  • You want biofeedback or a personalized program.

A pelvic-floor physical therapist can assess your technique, identify tension or weakness, and design a routine that fits your body.

Biofeedback #

Biofeedback uses sensors to show you what your pelvic floor is doing in real time. It can be helpful if you are not sure you are activating the right muscles, or if you are not progressing with home exercises.

A typical course involves an assessment, sensor placement, guided practice, and a home program. It is generally safe and often effective, especially when combined with behavioral techniques. Ask your clinician whether it is appropriate for you.

Key idea · Consistency over intensity

A few minutes of correct practice most days is better than an intense session once a week. Progress takes weeks to months, not days. Be patient, breathe, and relax as much as you squeeze.

D

Glossary

Plain-language definitions for the terms used in this book.

3 min read·748 words·Appendices

Sexual vocabulary is often vague, euphemistic, or inaccurate. This glossary uses direct language and notes where a term is contested or imprecise. It is not exhaustive, but it covers the concepts you will meet in these chapters.

TermMeaning
AftercareThe physical and emotional care given after sex: water, warmth, closeness, check-ins, and reassurance.
Anal sexSexual activity involving the anus. It requires explicit consent, relaxation, hygiene, and generous lubrication.
ArousalThe physical and psychological state of being sexually excited. It includes blood flow, lubrication, sensitivity, and changes in breathing and muscle tension.
Arousal non-concordanceWhen genital response (erection, lubrication) does not match subjective desire or consent. It is normal and important to understand.
Barrier methodA method that physically blocks contact, such as condoms, dental dams, or gloves.
CervixThe lower part of the uterus, at the top of the vagina. It can be sensitive, and deep penetration may be uncomfortable for some people.
ClitorisThe primary organ of sexual pleasure for most people with vulvas. The visible glans is only part of a larger internal structure.
ConsentA freely given, reversible, informed, enthusiastic, and specific agreement to a sexual act. It must be ongoing and can be withdrawn at any time.
CUV complexThe clitourethrovaginal complex: the internal clitoris, urethra, and front vaginal wall, which work together during arousal and penetration.
DesireThe motivation or interest in sex. It can be spontaneous (appearing without stimulation) or responsive (appearing after arousal or connection).
Dental damA thin sheet of latex or polyurethane used as a barrier during oral sex on a vulva or anus.
DyspareuniaPersistent or recurrent pain during sex. It is a medical symptom, not a personal failing, and it is treatable.
EdgingThe practice of approaching orgasm and then pausing or slowing down, often to build awareness and control.
Erectile dysfunction (ED)Difficulty getting or maintaining an erection sufficient for desired sexual activity. It can have physical and psychological causes.
ForeplaySexual activity before penetration — kissing, touch, oral, manual stimulation, teasing. It is sex, not merely a warm-up.
FRIESA consent model: Freely given, Reversible, Informed, Enthusiastic, Specific.
G-spotA popular term for a sensitive area on the front vaginal wall. Anatomical evidence for a discrete structure is inconsistent; it is better understood as part of the CUV complex.
GlansThe head of the clitoris or penis. It is highly sensitive.
KegelA pelvic-floor muscle exercise involving squeezing and lifting the muscles, then fully relaxing.
LabiaThe folds of skin around the vulva: the outer labia majora and inner labia minora. They vary widely in size, shape, and color.
LubricantA product used to reduce friction during sex. Water-based lubricant is compatible with most condoms and toys; silicone-based lubricant lasts longer but can damage silicone toys.
OrgasmA rhythmic release of sexual tension, often accompanied by involuntary muscle contractions and intense pleasure. It is not required for good sex.
Pelvic floorA hammock of muscles supporting the bladder, bowel, and reproductive organs. It plays a role in arousal, erection, ejaculation, orgasm, and continence.
PenetrationInsertion of a body part, toy, or object into an orifice. It is one sex act among many, not the definition of sex.
PerineumThe area between the genitals and the anus. It can be sensitive for people of all genders.
Premature ejaculation (PE)Ejaculation that happens sooner than desired, consistently, and causes distress. It is common and treatable.
ProstateA gland below the bladder that can be stimulated through the anal wall. It requires explicit consent, hygiene, and lubrication.
Responsive desireDesire that emerges after arousal, connection, or stimulation rather than spontaneously. It is common and normal.
Skene's glandsParaurethral glands near the urethra, homologous to the male prostate. They produce a small amount of fluid in some people during arousal or orgasm.
SpectatoringWatching yourself from the outside during sex, monitoring your performance instead of being present. It increases anxiety and reduces pleasure.
STISexually transmitted infection. Many STIs are asymptomatic; regular testing and barrier methods reduce risk.
UrethraThe tube that carries urine out of the body. It is separate from the vagina.
VaginaThe internal muscular canal. It is not the same as the vulva.
VulvaThe external genital area, including the mons, labia, clitoris, vestibule, and vaginal opening.

Note · Language changes

Sexual language is culturally specific and constantly evolving. If a term in this book does not fit your body or experience, use the words that do. The goal is clarity and respect, not conformity.

E

Resources and Further Reading

Trusted places to learn more, find a therapist, and check your assumptions.

2 min read·470 words·Appendices

Sexual health information ranges from excellent to dangerously misleading. The resources below are reputable starting points, not endorsements of every claim they make. Use them to learn, ask better questions, and find qualified professionals.

Note · Links change

Web addresses move. If a link stops working, search for the organization or title rather than assuming the resource is gone.

Sexual health organizations #

  • Planned Parenthood — clear, practical information on consent, contraception, STIs, anatomy, and relationships. plannedparenthood.org
  • NHS Sexual Health — UK-based, evidence-informed guidance on sexual health and relationships. nhs.uk/conditions/sexual-health
  • Mayo Clinic — clinical overviews of sexual health conditions, treatments, and when to see a doctor. mayoclinic.org
  • CDC Sexual Health — public-health guidance on STIs, testing, and prevention. cdc.gov/sexualhealth
  • Kinsey Institute — research and resources on sexuality, relationships, and sexual health. kinseyinstitute.org

Therapy and professional support #

  • AASECT — the American Association of Sexuality Educators, Counselors, and Therapists. A directory of certified professionals. aasect.org
  • Psychology Today Therapist Directory — search for sex therapists and relationship counselors by location. psychologytoday.com/us/therapists
  • Inclusive Therapists — a directory focused on affirming care for marginalized communities. inclusivetherapists.com
  • Pelvic-floor physical therapy — search for a pelvic-health specialist in your area. A referral from a gynecologist, urologist, or primary-care clinician can help.

Books #

  • Emily Nagoski — Come as You Are — a research-informed book on female sexuality, desire, and arousal.
  • Paul Joannides — The Guide to Getting It On — a comprehensive, practical, and often funny guide to sex.
  • Marty Klein — Sexual Intelligence — a thoughtful book on desire, communication, and letting go of performance pressure.
  • Esther Perel — Mating in Captivity — a nuanced exploration of desire and long-term relationships.
  • Jen Gunter — The Vagina Bible — evidence-based information on vulvovaginal health.
  • Aaron Spitz — The Penis Book — a urologist's guide to male sexual health.

Podcasts and audio #

  • Sex with Emily — practical, sex-positive advice and interviews.
  • Where Should We Begin? with Esther Perel — real couples therapy sessions, including issues of desire and intimacy.
  • The Kinsey Institute's research updates — accessible summaries of current sexuality research.

Consent and communication #

  • Planned Parenthood's consent resources — clear explanations of consent, FRIES, and healthy relationships.
  • The Consent Workshop — educational resources on consent, boundaries, and communication.
  • RAINN — support for survivors of sexual violence. rainn.org

When to seek medical care #

See a healthcare provider if you experience:

  • Pain during sex that persists or recurs.
  • Sudden changes in erection, ejaculation, or orgasm.
  • Genital pain, sores, discharge, or unusual odors.
  • Symptoms of a urinary tract infection or STI.
  • Concerns about hormones, medication side effects, or chronic illness.
  • Distress about sex that affects your daily life or relationship.

A good clinician will take you seriously. If yours does not, find another one.

Key idea · Keep learning

No single book, article, or expert has the final word on sex. Stay curious, check your sources, and treat your partner as the most important expert on their own body.
